chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar from Muhammad ibn Isma'il from Ibn Abi Umayr from Umar ibn Udhaynah from Zurarah who said:

I asked him about a man who wrote to his wife [a letter of] her divorce, or wrote [a letter of] freeing his slave, and his tongue did not speak it. He said: 'It is not [valid] until he speaks it with his tongue.'
ai.seo_question: Is a written divorce letter valid if the husband does not speak the words of divorce?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that written declarations of divorce or manumission are not legally binding until verbally articulated, highlighting the Shia juristic emphasis on the spoken word (*qawl*) as the primary vehicle for legal intent (*niyyah*) in these acts. This ruling distinguishes between mere written intent and the formal execution of the act, a principle often debated in *usul al-fiqh* regarding the sufficiency of writing (*kitabah*) versus speech (*nuthur*). The context of Chapter 40, while primarily focusing on childbirth and *aqiqah*, places this legal nuance within the broader framework of family law and personal status regulations.
